readerTitle: The one-page list that cut surgical deaths in eight hospitals
caseNote: 실제 사례 (WHO 수술 안전 체크리스트, Haynes et al. 2009 NEJM, Urbach et al. 2014 NEJM) + 가상 적용 (IT 서비스 회사의 서버 이전, 사내 재무팀 월말 결산)
insight: 좋은 체크리스트는 기억을 돕는 목록이 아니다. 실수가 비싼 순간에 팀을 멈춰 세우고 서로 말하게 만드는 장치다.
misconception: 체크리스트는 꼼꼼할수록 좋고, 도입해서 서명만 받으면 효과가 난다.

sources.text: Haynes, A.B. et al. (2009). A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population. New England Journal of Medicine, 360:491–499.
World Health Organization, Surgical Safety Checklist and the Safe Surgery Saves Lives programme (2008–2009)
Urbach, D.R. et al. (2014). Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada. New England Journal of Medicine, 370:1029–1038.
Gawande, A. (2009). The Checklist Manifesto. Metropolitan Books.

factChecks.note: Haynes 2009: 8개 도시 8개 병원(토론토, 뉴델리, 암만, 오클랜드, 마닐라, 이파카라, 런던, 시애틀). 사망률 1.5% → 0.8%, 입원 중 합병증 11.0% → 7.0%. 논문 초록으로 다시 확인하세요. 무작위 대조 시험이 아닌 전후 비교 연구라는 점을 카드 4에 적었습니다.
체크리스트 구성: 19개 항목, 세 번의 멈춤(Sign in 마취 전, Time out 절개 전, Sign out 수술실 퇴실 전). Time out에 팀원 이름·역할 소개, 항생제 투여 확인이 포함됩니다. WHO 2009 공식 체크리스트 PDF로 확인하세요.
Urbach 2014: 온타리오주 병원에서 체크리스트 의무화 전후로 사망률과 합병증에 유의한 감소가 없었다는 결과. 원인(형식적 이행, 이미 낮은 기준치 등)은 연구자와 논평자의 해석이므로 카드에 '가능한 이유'로만 적었습니다.
항공 체크리스트에서 착안했다는 점, 팀 소개가 이후 문제 제기를 쉽게 한다는 주장은 Gawande(2009) 책의 설명입니다. 수치 없이 정성적으로만 썼습니다.

cards.title: The one-page list that cut surgical deaths in eight hospitals
body: In 2008, a World Health Organization team tested a single sheet of paper in eight hospitals, from Seattle and London to New Delhi and Ifakara, Tanzania.
No new equipment. No new drugs. Just 19 checks spoken aloud. Afterward, the death rate among surgery patients in the study nearly halved.

image.label: A one-page checklist on a tray in an operating room
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 수술실 기구 트레이 위에 종이 한 장짜리 체크리스트가 놓여 있고, 뒤로 마스크 쓴 의료진 세 명이 둘러서 있음. 피나 상처 묘사 없이 밝고 차분한 톤. 실제 기관 로고(WHO 등)는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How would you design it?
body: You're on the team. Surgeons, nurses and anesthetists are highly trained experts. Yet basic steps still get skipped: an antibiotic given late, a missing scan, a team that never discussed what could go wrong.
What kind of tool do you build?

options.text: A thorough checklist covering every step of the operation
options.feedback: It looks complete, but busy experts skim long lists or skip them. The few steps that matter most get buried among the obvious ones.

options.text: A short list read aloud at a few key moments, including team introductions
options.feedback: It costs a couple of minutes and targets only the steps people miss. Speaking aloud also gets the whole team talking. That's what the WHO team chose.

options.text: No list. Better training and reminder posters instead
options.feedback: Training raises skill, but these experts already know the steps. The problem is skipping them under pressure, which training alone rarely fixes.

cards.title: Three pauses, 19 checks.
body: Each pause takes a minute or two. Many items look obvious. They're on the list because, on a busy day, people skip them.

breakdown.label: Before anesthesia
breakdown.detail: Right patient, right site, allergies, airway risk

breakdown.label: Before the first cut
breakdown.detail: Everyone says name and role; antibiotic given; risks discussed

breakdown.label: Before leaving the room
breakdown.detail: Instruments and sponges counted, samples labeled

cards.title: Fewer deaths, fewer complications.
body: The study compared nearly 4,000 patients before the checklist with a similar number after. Results improved at rich and poor hospitals alike.
It was a before-and-after study, not a randomized trial, so other changes may have helped too.

cards.title: The pause-point checklist
body: A **pause-point checklist** stops the team at the moments when a mistake is costly and hard to undo, and makes them confirm a few critical things out loud.
It doesn't teach experts their job. It catches the steps they skip under pressure. The idea came partly from aviation, where pilots run short checks before takeoff.
Atul Gawande, who led the work, argued that the introductions mattered too. Once people have spoken, they find it easier to **speak up** later.

image.label: A timeline with three stop signs
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 시작부터 끝까지 선이 이어지고, 되돌리기 어려운 지점 세 곳에 작은 멈춤 표지판. 각 표지판 옆에 말풍선 아이콘(팀이 소리 내어 확인한다는 뜻). 의료 장면 묘사 없이 추상적으로.

cards.title: Every business has its time out.
body: Look for moments that are expensive to reverse: a job leaving the factory, a contract going out, a price change going live.
A finance team inside a large company might pause once before closing the month: Are all bank accounts matched? Did anyone post an unusual entry? Does anyone have a concern?
cards.callout: Short list, right moment, said out loud.
cards.softwareNote: Many teams hold a go/no-go check before a release: rollback plan ready, monitoring on, someone on call. It works for the same reason the time out does.

cards.title: A mandated checklist can become a ritual.
body: In 2010, Ontario, Canada required surgical checklists in its hospitals. A 2014 study of more than 100 hospitals found no meaningful drop in deaths or complications afterward.
Possible reasons: some teams ticked boxes without truly pausing, and rates were already low. The paper was the same. How people used it was not.
A checklist works only if leaders treat the pause as real and anyone can stop the job.

cards.title: Now it's an IT services firm.
body: You move clients' systems to new servers over weekends. Last month a job failed because nobody confirmed the backup had finished. The client was furious.

options.text: A 70-item migration checklist, signed off by email after each job
options.feedback: Thorough on paper, but signed after the fact it records mistakes instead of stopping them. Long lists also invite box-ticking.

options.text: A short go/no-go call before cutover: backup confirmed, rollback ready, anyone can say stop
options.feedback: It adds a few minutes at the one moment that's hard to undo, and gives junior engineers a clear time to raise concerns.

options.text: Send your most senior engineer to every migration
options.feedback: Experience helps, but it doesn't scale and experts skip steps too. A pause protects every job, not just the ones your best person can attend.

cards.title: Make the team stop and talk where mistakes are costly.
body: The checklist worked because it was short, timed to the right moments and spoken aloud. Without a real pause, it's just paper.
**Try it today:** find one step in your work that's hard to undo. Write three checks for it, and say them aloud with your team next time.
